nimacimab.summary: An experimental anti-CB1 antibody in Phase 2 for obesity, aimed at lowering appetite and fat storage for a leaner body.

quick.overview:
Nimacimab is an antibody drug that blocks the cannabinoid-1 (CB1) receptor, a target involved in appetite and metabolism. The payoff people follow it for is fat loss and a leaner look.

It binds CB1 from outside the cell and was designed to act mainly in peripheral tissue, avoiding the psychiatric effects seen with earlier brain-penetrant CB1 blockers. A Phase 2 obesity trial that began in 2024 tests it alone and alongside semaglutide against placebo; no published results were found.
quick.how: Nimacimab is not available outside clinical trials, so there is no everyday routine. Fat-loss followers track it as one of several new anti-obesity drug targets, and the registered trial pairs it with semaglutide.
quick.risks: Its safety profile is not established in published form. It is not approved anywhere and is available only within clinical trials. Earlier brain-penetrant CB1 blockers were withdrawn over psychiatric side effects, which is the reason for its peripheral design.

angle.text: Nimacimab is an anti-CB1 antibody that fat-loss followers track as a peripherally acting obesity drug. By blocking CB1 it aims to lower appetite and fat storage, leading to weight loss and a leaner look. It is in a Phase 2 obesity trial.

nad-injections.summary: Injected or infused NAD+ is used in longevity clinics for energy and anti-aging, with users hoping for fresher, more youthful-looking skin.

quick.overview:
NAD+ is a coenzyme every cell uses for metabolism. Some clinics sell injections or infusions of it for anti-aging, energy and recovery, and people use it hoping for fresher skin and a more youthful look.

NAD+ carries electrons in metabolic reactions and is used by sirtuin, PARP and CD38 enzymes. Proponents say injecting it raises levels that fall with age; reference sources note that human evidence for that decline is inconsistent. Registered human trials of injectable NAD+ address specific medical conditions such as hematopoietic recovery, hearing loss and vascular aging.
quick.how: It is given at wellness and longevity clinics as an injection or an IV infusion, often as part of a broader anti-aging or energy package. Users describe it as a periodic treatment and report effects on energy and how they feel.
quick.risks: Experts quoted in reference works say the long-term safety of intravenous NAD+ is unknown. It is not licensed as a medicine in the UK. Clinic marketing claims for aging and appearance have not been tested in controlled human trials.

angle.text: Longevity clinics and online communities promote injected NAD+ to raise cellular NAD+ levels, with the aim of better cellular energy and repair and fresher, more youthful-looking skin. The appearance claim rests on cell biology and user reports; registered human trials address other conditions.

glutathione-injections.summary: Injected glutathione, often with vitamin C, is used in some countries to lighten skin and even out tone.

quick.overview:
Glutathione is an antioxidant peptide the body makes. Some clinics and online communities use injections or IV drips of it, often with vitamin C, to lighten skin and even out tone.

Proponents say glutathione reduces melanin production, and that injection avoids its poor oral absorption. Reference sources confirm oral absorption is poor; a 2019 systematic review described its effectiveness for skin lightening as unclear, and no controlled trial of injected glutathione for general skin lightening was found.
quick.how: It is given as a course of IV drips or injections at clinics, commonly paired with vitamin C. Users report results building over repeated sessions, and it is popular for skin brightening in several countries.
quick.risks: The Philippine government recommends against intravenous glutathione because of possible side effects. No controlled safety data for cosmetic injection were found.

angle.text: Injected glutathione, often paired with vitamin C, is used to lighten skin and even out tone. The idea is that the antioxidant lowers melanin production, giving lighter pigment and a brighter, more even complexion. Evidence for skin lightening comes from small studies, and a 2019 review called effectiveness unclear.

vip-vasoactive-intestinal-peptide.summary: A natural vasodilating neuropeptide sold as a research peptide; users speculate it could aid circulation and recovery.

quick.overview:
VIP is a natural 28-amino-acid peptide that widens blood vessels, relaxes smooth muscle and modulates immune activity. Users interested in recovery speculate it could improve circulation and help them train and heal better.

It binds VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors, raising cyclic AMP in target cells, and its half-life in blood is about two minutes. Human trials of VIP are small and aimed at physiology, headache or lung disease; none tests it for appearance or recovery.
quick.how: VIP is sold by some vendors as a research peptide and discussed in peptide communities alongside other recovery compounds. There is no established routine, and its short half-life is part of the discussion around how it is used.
quick.risks: Intravenous VIP was used in migraine studies to provoke headache, showing it has vascular effects. No safety data exist for the research-peptide use pattern, and it is not an approved product.

angle.text: VIP is a natural vasodilating neuropeptide sold as a research peptide. Users speculate that widening blood vessels and modulating immune activity could speed recovery, supporting better training and healing. Its established research concerns gut, lung and immune function.

aviptadil.summary: Synthetic VIP used with phentolamine for erectile dysfunction in some countries and tested in COVID-19 lung failure.

quick.overview:
Aviptadil is a lab-made version of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). In some European countries it is used with phentolamine as an injection for erectile dysfunction, and peptide communities mention it alongside VIP for circulation and recovery.

It activates VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors, producing vasodilation and anti-inflammatory effects. It was also tested for COVID-19 respiratory failure; the large TESICO trial, published in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine in 2023, showed no significant improvement in outcomes versus placebo according to a reference summary.
quick.how: Its established use is as a combination injection with phentolamine for erectile dysfunction in some countries. In peptide communities it is mentioned as a synthetic counterpart to VIP; no appearance routine has been studied.
quick.risks: Safety data come from patient trials in erectile dysfunction and critical illness. It is not approved for any lung indication in the US, and no data exist for use in healthy people.

angle.text: Aviptadil is synthetic VIP that widens blood vessels, used with phentolamine as an injection for erectile dysfunction in some European countries. Peptide communities mention it alongside VIP for circulation and recovery. It has been tested in COVID-19 lung failure; no appearance use has been studied.

ara-290.summary: An EPO-derived repair peptide tested in small neuropathy trials, discussed by users for tissue protection and recovery.

quick.overview:
ARA 290 (cibinetide) is a short peptide derived from erythropoietin, designed to trigger tissue-protective signalling without boosting red blood cells. Recovery-focused users discuss it for tissue protection and nerve healing.

It is designed to activate the innate repair receptor, which researchers describe as mediating tissue protection and anti-inflammation, while avoiding the hematologic effects of EPO. Small exploratory trials in sarcoidosis and type 2 diabetes neuropathy reported symptom and nerve-fibre improvements.
quick.how: It is investigational and has no approved use. In peptide communities it is discussed as a repair-oriented compound for recovery, though human data come from small patient trials rather than healthy trainees.
quick.risks: Safety data come from small patient trials. It is investigational with no approved use, and its effects in healthy people have not been studied.

angle.text: ARA 290 is an EPO-derived peptide that activates a tissue repair receptor, and recovery-focused users discuss it for faster tissue healing and better recovery between sessions. It has been tested in small neuropathy trials in sarcoidosis and diabetes.

b7-33.summary: A lab-made relaxin mimic studied in animals for fibrosis; peptide communities discuss it for tissue repair and scar reduction.

quick.overview:
B7-33 is a short peptide designed to imitate part of the hormone relaxin-2, which has anti-fibrotic and blood-vessel-relaxing effects. Peptide communities discuss it for tissue repair and smoother, less scarred healing.

It binds the relaxin receptor RXFP1 but is functionally selective, activating ERK1/2 signalling more than cAMP. Published findings are from cell, mouse and rat studies, mainly of heart and kidney fibrosis and vascular function; no human trial has been published.
quick.how: It appears in peptide-vendor catalogues under recovery and tissue repair. There is no documented appearance routine, and it exists mainly as a research compound.
quick.risks: Human safety is unstudied. It is not an approved drug anywhere; availability is limited to research-chemical channels.

angle.text: B7-33 is a lab-made relaxin mimic that reduces fibrosis in animal studies, and peptide communities speculate that it could mean less scarring and smoother tissue remodeling and healing. All published work is in cells and rodents.

pe-22-28.summary: A spadin-derived peptide studied in rodents as a fast-acting antidepressant; some users discuss it for mood and confidence.

quick.overview:
PE-22-28 is a short peptide trimmed down from spadin, a natural fragment that blocks the TREK-1 potassium channel. Some peptide users discuss it for a mood lift, mental sharpness and the confidence that goes with it.

It inhibits the TREK-1 channel, which helps set neurons' resting potential, and blocking it is proposed to produce antidepressant-like effects. It was designed to last longer and act more strongly than spadin; rodent experiments report antidepressant-like effects after short dosing periods, and no human trials have been published.
quick.how: It is available as a research chemical and discussed in peptide communities as a mood-related compound. No established routine exists in people.
quick.risks: Human safety is unknown. It is not approved for any use and is available only as a research chemical.

angle.text: PE-22-28 is a spadin-derived peptide that blocks the TREK-1 channel and has shown antidepressant-like effects in rodents. Some users discuss it for a mood lift and better confidence and presence. No direct appearance use is documented.

pnc-27.summary: A p53-derived peptide reported to rupture cancer cells in lab studies, sold as a research chemical to longevity-minded users.

quick.overview:
PNC-27 fuses a piece of the p53 tumour-suppressor protein to a cell-penetrating sequence. Longevity-minded users are interested in it because lab experiments report that it ruptures cancer cells while sparing normal ones.

It is reported to bind HDM-2 protein displayed on cancer-cell membranes and form pores that cause the cell to burst. All published evidence is from cell lines and laboratory models; no human trial has been published.
quick.how: It is sold by research-peptide vendors and listed among longevity-oriented peptides. No appearance use is documented.
quick.risks: Human safety is unstudied. It is not an approved drug; it is sold as a research chemical.

angle.text: PNC-27 is a p53-derived peptide that lyses cancer cells in laboratory studies, and longevity-minded users follow it as a general-health compound. All published evidence is from cell lines; no appearance use is documented.

erythropoietin.summary: A kidney hormone and anaemia drug used for endurance doping; raises red blood cells for stamina, with serious cardiovascular warnings.

quick.overview:
Erythropoietin (EPO) is the hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells. Injectable versions treat anaemia in kidney disease and chemotherapy patients, and some physique users discuss it for stamina and recovery capacity in training.

It binds the EPO receptor on red-cell precursors, activating JAK2 signalling to increase red blood cell production and oxygen-carrying capacity. It is known mostly as an endurance-sport doping agent; clinical trials reviewed were in anaemic patients, and none aimed at appearance.
quick.how: Medically it is prescribed as an injectable for anaemia. In endurance sport it has been used to raise red cell mass, and in physique circles it is mentioned as a way to train harder and longer.
quick.risks: It is a prescription-only drug. Reported risks in patients include serious cardiovascular events and increased mortality in some groups, and it is banned in competitive sport.

angle.text: Erythropoietin raises red blood cell count, increasing oxygen delivery so users can train harder and longer, which some physique users link to more muscle and leanness. Its performance effects are studied in endurance athletes; a direct effect on muscle or appearance has not been tested.

abaloparatide.summary: An approved osteoporosis bone-builder that forum users discuss for facial structure and height alongside bonesmashing and lengthening.

quick.overview:
Abaloparatide (Tymlos) is a prescription injectable that stimulates bone formation. Looksmaxxing forums discuss it alongside bonesmashing, puberty and limb lengthening, hoping for thicker facial bone and a stronger jaw and cheekbone structure.

It is a synthetic analogue of parathyroid hormone-related protein that activates the PTH1 receptor, increasing osteoblast activity and new bone formation. The phase 3 ACTIVE trial reported fewer new vertebral fractures versus placebo in postmenopausal women; no published study tests it for facial bone, height or appearance.
quick.how: Its approved use is as an injectable for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and men at high fracture risk. Forum use is theoretical or anecdotal and is discussed as a complement to bone-focused or lengthening approaches.
quick.risks: The label lists osteosarcoma risk, low blood pressure on standing, high calcium and allergic reactions, and advises avoiding it with open growth plates. It is prescription-only and approved for osteoporosis, not for appearance.

angle.text: Abaloparatide is an approved osteoporosis drug that builds bone by activating the PTH1 receptor, and forum users speculate it could thicken facial bone for a stronger jaw and cheekbone structure. Trials have studied it for fracture risk in osteoporosis; none address facial bone or appearance.

salmon-calcitonin.summary: A fish-derived calcitonin used for Paget's disease and high blood calcium that slows bone breakdown to preserve bone.

quick.overview:
Salmon calcitonin is a prescription peptide that slows bone breakdown. Doctors use it for Paget's disease of bone, high blood calcium and, when other drugs are unsuitable, postmenopausal osteoporosis, and bone-focused readers mention it as a way to preserve bone.

It activates calcitonin receptors on bone-resorbing osteoclasts, reducing bone breakdown and calcium release. It is a bone-resorption inhibitor rather than a bone-building agent, and the label notes fracture-reduction efficacy has not been demonstrated for osteoporosis.
quick.how: It is used under medical supervision as an injection for its approved conditions. No looksmaxxing routine or appearance study was found.
quick.risks: The label lists anaphylaxis, low calcium, nausea, flushing and a possible increased malignancy risk. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Salmon calcitonin slows bone breakdown, so bone-focused readers mention it as a way to preserve bone and support structure. It is used for Paget's disease and high blood calcium; it has not been studied for facial structure.

osteocalcin.summary: A bone-made protein and proposed hormone linked to bone formation, insulin and muscle in animal studies.

quick.overview:
Osteocalcin is a protein made by bone-building cells, and doctors use its blood level as a marker of how actively bone is forming. Bone-focused readers connect it to bone strength and metabolism.

Since 2007, mouse studies have proposed that it also acts as a hormone on insulin, muscle and testosterone, with the uncarboxylated form signalling through receptors such as GPRC6A and GPR158. Human relevance is still being investigated, and no studies test it for looks.
quick.how: It is not a marketed product. In practice people encounter it as a blood test of bone formation, and discussion of it centres on supporting the bone and vitamin K pathways that produce it.
quick.risks: No approved therapeutic use or safety data for administering it are described. Human studies reviewed measure it as a marker rather than as a treatment.

angle.text: Osteocalcin is a bone-made protein and proposed hormone, and bone-focused readers connect it to stronger bone structure and metabolic benefits. It is studied as a marker of bone formation and, in animals, for effects on insulin and muscle; no looks-related use has been tested in humans.

irisin.summary: A proposed exercise hormone released from muscle that turns white fat brown-like in mice, linking training to leanness.

quick.overview:
Irisin is a protein proposed in 2012 to be released by exercising muscle and to turn white fat toward a brown-fat-like, heat-producing state, burning more calories. Fat-loss readers cite it as a way exercise might make you leaner.

It is cleaved from the membrane protein FNDC5, whose production rises with muscle PGC-1-alpha, and cell and animal studies propose signalling through alpha-V integrin receptors. The browning finding comes from mice; researchers have disputed how reliably irisin can be measured in people, and human studies mainly measure blood levels.
quick.how: There is no product; people associate irisin with regular exercise as the thing that raises it. Discussion centres on training as the lever.
quick.risks: No approved product exists and no human safety data for administering irisin are described in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Irisin is a proposed exercise hormone: muscle releases it during training, and in mice it turns white fat brown-like and raises energy expenditure, pointing to a leaner look. Human evidence is limited and disputed.

adropin.summary: A liver and brain peptide linked in mice to fat and glucose metabolism; human data are blood-level associations.

quick.overview:
Adropin is a small peptide made mostly in the liver and brain, and fat-loss readers discuss it as a possible metabolic lever for fat loss and a leaner look. In mice, low levels go with more body fat and insulin resistance, and giving it improved glucose handling.

It is cleaved from the ENHO gene product, and its expression follows feeding and the body clock; GPR19 has been proposed as its receptor. In people, lower blood levels have been associated with obesity and heart disease, but no trials test adropin as a way to change body fat.
quick.how: There is no approved product. Discussion focuses on feeding, the body clock and metabolic health as the factors that shape its levels.
quick.risks: No approved product exists and the sources reviewed give no human safety data for administering it.

angle.text: Adropin is a liver and brain peptide that shapes fat and glucose metabolism in mice, and fat-loss readers see it as a possible way to improve fuel use and get leaner. Human data are blood-level associations with obesity and heart disease.

asprosin.summary: A fat-derived fasting hormone that raises glucose and appetite in mice; high levels track with obesity.

quick.overview:
Asprosin is a hormone released from fat tissue during fasting. In mice it tells the liver to release glucose and the brain to increase appetite, so fat-loss readers follow it as a possible appetite target, where blocking it could ease weight gain.

It is cleaved from fibrillin-1 by furin; reported receptors include OLFR734/OR4M1 in the liver and PTPRD in the brain, and antibodies against it lowered weight in mouse models. People with obesity or diabetes tend to have higher levels, while people with a rare syndrome of low asprosin are very lean.
quick.how: There is no product to use; interest centres on antibody-based approaches that lower it, which have been shown in mice only.
quick.risks: No approved product exists and no human safety data for administering or blocking it are described in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Asprosin is a fasting hormone from fat that raises glucose and appetite in mice, so fat-loss readers follow it as a target where lowering it could mean lower intake and easier leanness. High levels track with obesity; no appearance use exists.

obestatin.summary: A ghrelin-gene peptide first reported in 2005 to curb appetite; follow-up work has questioned both the effect and its receptor.

quick.overview:
Obestatin is a peptide made from the same gene as the hunger hormone ghrelin. A 2005 paper in Science reported that it reduced appetite in rodents, which led fat-loss readers to see it as a possible diet aid for lower intake and fat loss.

Other labs could not confirm the appetite effect, and its proposed receptor GPR39 was later found to respond to zinc instead. No studies test it for weight or appearance in people.
quick.how: There is no product; it is discussed as a hormone of the appetite system rather than something people use.
quick.risks: No approved product exists and the sources reviewed give no human safety data for administering it.

angle.text: Obestatin is a ghrelin-gene peptide first reported to curb appetite, so fat-loss readers see it as a possible diet aid for lower intake and fat loss. Later studies could not reproduce the appetite effect, and its receptor is disputed.

limostatin.summary: A fruit-fly hormone that lowers insulin during fasting, studied as a model for how fasting signals shape fat handling.

quick.overview:
Limostatin is a signalling peptide discovered in fruit flies. When food is scarce, gut endocrine cells release it and it tells insulin-producing cells to release less insulin; metabolism-minded readers cite it as a model for how fasting signals fat handling and leanness.

It was the first well-characterised example of a fasting-induced hormone that opposes insulin. In the original 2015 study, flies lacking limostatin developed high insulin, low blood sugar and extra body fat. The published work is confined to flies and laboratory models.
quick.how: There is no product or routine; it appears in fat-loss and metabolism peptide lists because of its insulin-lowering role.
quick.risks: No human safety or efficacy data have been published, and effects in people have not been tested.

angle.text: Limostatin is a fruit-fly hormone that suppresses insulin during fasting, and metabolism-minded readers cite it as a model for how fasting changes fat storage signals and could lead to a leaner body. It has been studied only in insects.

alamandine.summary: A blood-pressure-regulating peptide of the renin-angiotensin system, studied in rodents for heart and vessel protection.

quick.overview:
Alamandine is a small peptide made in the body as part of the renin-angiotensin system, described in 2013. Longevity-minded readers discuss it for heart, vessel and tissue protection.

It is generated by ACE2 from angiotensin A or from angiotensin-(1-7) and signals mainly through the MrgD receptor, producing vasorelaxation and protection against cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis in animals. Evidence comes from cell and rodent experiments; no human trials have tested it.
quick.how: There is no approved product or established routine. It is listed among longevity-category peptides.
quick.risks: No human safety data exist. Because it influences blood pressure and vascular tone in animals, effects in people are unstudied. It is not an approved drug.

angle.text: Alamandine is a renin-angiotensin peptide that lowers blood pressure and protects heart tissue in rodents, so longevity-minded readers discuss it for heart and vessel health. It has not been tested in humans, and no appearance use exists.

thyrotropin-releasing-hormone.summary: The hypothalamic hormone that tells the pituitary to release TSH, setting thyroid activity, metabolism and energy.

quick.overview:
TRH is a three-amino-acid hormone made in the hypothalamus. It signals the pituitary to release TSH and prolactin, which control the thyroid, so it sits at the top of the thyroid axis that sets metabolism and energy. Hormone-minded readers discuss it for thyroid, mood and energy effects.

TRH binds receptors on pituitary thyrotroph cells and is cleared within minutes; in the brain it influences arousal and neurotransmitter release. Its discoverers shared the 1977 Nobel Prize, and clinical use has been mainly diagnostic, with human studies for other conditions small or dated.
quick.how: Clinically it is used as a diagnostic test of the thyroid axis. In peptide lists it appears in the recovery category because of brain effects seen in research.
quick.risks: Reported effects of injected TRH include nausea, flushing and a mild blood pressure rise. Because it raises TSH and prolactin, endocrine effects are expected, and it has not been established as a treatment for the conditions studied.

angle.text: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone sits at the top of the thyroid axis: it signals the pituitary to release TSH, raising thyroid activity that shapes metabolism and energy. Hormone-minded readers discuss it for thyroid, mood and energy effects; human studies outside diagnostics are small and dated.
